collections.title: Paintings from the Art Institute of Chicago
collections.summary: Twenty-four public-domain paintings, from El Greco to Mondrian, with the museum’s own descriptions.

entries.title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884
entries.creator: Georges Seurat
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: For his largest and best-known painting, Georges Seurat depicted Parisians enjoying all sorts of leisurely activities—strolling, lounging, sailing, and fishing—in the park called La Grande Jatte on the River Seine. He used an innovative technique called Pointillism that was inspired by optical and color theory, applying tiny dabs of different colored paint that viewers would see as a single, and Seurat believed, more brilliant hue.

entries.title: The Bedroom
entries.creator: Vincent van Gogh
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: In 1888, Van Gogh moved into his own home in Arles, France. He dubbed it the “Studio of the South,” hoping that fellow artists would join him there to work. This is one of three versions he painted of his beloved Arles bedroom. While its vivid palette and dramatic perspective seem to burst with nervous vitality, Van Gogh intended the painting "to express utter repose."

entries.title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
entries.creator: Gustave Caillebotte
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: Considered Caillebotte’s masterpiece, this view of a busy intersection captures both an everyday moment and all that was new in a rapidly changing Paris. The clothes are the latest fashion. The retractable umbrella was just invented. And a decades-long renovation had transformed the medieval streets of Paris into grand boulevards, like the ones seen here. It's a painting you want to walk into.

entries.title: Water Lilies
entries.creator: Claude Monet
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago

entries.title: Stacks of Wheat (End of Summer)
entries.creator: Claude Monet
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago

entries.title: Two Sisters (On the Terrace)
entries.creator: Pierre-Auguste Renoir
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: Despite the title, the young women in this painting were not actually sisters. The older girl in the center gazes absently beyond her younger companion, whose red cheeks suggest that she just dashed into the picture. These casual expressions make this “sisterly” moment feel genuine. Renoir juxtaposed the girls’ figures against a dreamy landscape, the basket of yarn evoking an artist’s palette.

entries.title: Self-Portrait
entries.creator: Vincent van Gogh
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: Van Gogh’s face is as well known as his art—in fact, it is inseparable from it. The artist painted more than 35 self-portraits over his lifetime. This one was created in Paris under the influence of Seurat and pointillism. The intense dabs of paint and color, anchored by his eyes, create a turbulent energy, giving the viewer a deep sense of the artist’s presence.

entries.title: At the Moulin Rouge
entries.creator: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: Toulouse-Lautrec made a career depicting colorful personalities from Parisian cabarets and dance halls like the Moulin Rouge. He populated this painting with that nightclub's regulars, including himself—the diminutive figure in the center background. Dancer La Goulue arranges her hair behind the table where Jane Avril, another performer, socializes. Singer May Milton peers out from the painting's right edge, her face harshly lit and acid green.

entries.title: Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare
entries.creator: Claude Monet
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: The Impressionists frequently paid tribute to the modern aspects of Paris, depicting scenes of grand boulevards and modern constructions. Monet made 12 paintings of the Gare Saint-Lazare. Here, he focused on the glass-and-iron train shed, where he found an appealing combination of artificial and natural effects: the rising steam of locomotives trapped within the structure and daylight penetrating the large, glazed sections of the roof.

entries.title: Woman at Her Toilette
entries.creator: Berthe Morisot
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: Rendered with feathery brushstrokes in shades of lavender, pink, blue, white, and gray, this Impressionist painting captures a subject often explored by male artists of the day but seldom broached by the period's few women artists. Morisot presents a decidely female perspective, intimate yet not eroticized. She signed her name along the bottom of the mirror, as if to suggest that the image in her painting is as ephemeral as a silvery reﬂection.

entries.title: Distant View of Niagara Falls
entries.creator: Thomas Cole
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: By the 19th century, Niagara Falls was already an iconic American landscape, nearly verging on mythical. Thomas Cole visited the landmark in May 1829 and composed this romanticized, autumnal scene the following year. In amplifying the natural grandeur of the American landscape, the artist wilfully ommitted the factories, scenic overlooks, and hotels that populated the area in the early 19th century.

entries.title: The Beach at Sainte-Adresse
entries.creator: Claude Monet
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: In 1867 Monet stayed with his aunt in Sainte-Adresse, a suburb of the port city of Le Havre in Normandy, where the artist grew up. Monet began the painting outdoors but likely revised it in his studio. Technical analysis of the work revealed that it started as a beach scene of yachts and tourists but ultimately became a view of sailboats and local fishermen.

entries.title: Improvisation No. 30 (Cannons)
entries.creator: Vasily Kandinsky
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: In his 1912 book Concerning the Spiritual in Art, Vasily Kandinsky advocated for an art that could move beyond imitation of the physical world, inspiring, as he put it, “vibrations in the soul.” Between 1910 and 1914 he produced a series of “improvisations," which he described as unconscious, spontaneous expressions. This painting—one of his first improvisations—is a standout work within the museum's modern art collection.

entries.title: The Herring Net
entries.creator: Winslow Homer
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: One of the most influential American painters of the 19th century, Winslow Homer is known for his dynamic depictions of both upper-class leisure pursuits and nature's power and beauty. The paintings he created after 1882 focus almost exclusively on humankind’s contest with nature. Here, Homer depicted the heroic efforts of fishermen hauling in an abundant catch of herring while steadying their boat amid turbulent swells.

entries.title: The Girl by the Window
entries.creator: Edvard Munch
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: Edvard Munch’s life and art have come to epitomize modern notions of anxiety. Created the same year as his renowned The Scream, this painting depicts a young girl in her nightgown gazing out at the city from her darkened room. The steep angle of the floor and the deep shadows that obliterate almost everything in the room create an unsettling and enigmatic scene.

entries.title: The Fountain, Villa Torlonia, Frascati, Italy
entries.creator: John Singer Sargent
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: The year 1907 was a turning point for Sargent; the sought-after portraitist stepped away from his successful portraiture career to pursue plein-air landscape painting. This work, depicting his traveling companions and fellow artists Wilfrid and Jane Emmet de Glehn, captures that moment of transition. Combining landscape and portraiture, the composition speaks to friendship and painterly pursuits while also celebrating color, light, and movement.

entries.title: Lozenge Composition with Yellow, Black, Blue, Red, and Gray
entries.creator: Piet Mondrian
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: Piet Mondrian, a founding member of the international movement De Stijl (the Style), said “the straight line tells the truth.” Deceptively simple, his works are the result of continual tinkering to achieve absolute balance and harmony. In this work, Mondrian rotated a square canvas 90 degrees to create a dynamic relationship between the rectilinear composition and the diagonal lines of the painting's edges.

entries.title: Nocturne: Blue and Gold—Southampton Water
entries.creator: James McNeill Whistler
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: In the 1870s James McNeill Whistler took a radical step toward abstraction with his "Nocturnes" series. In keeping with his art-for-art’s-sake creed, these works capture the stillness of evening while evoking the artistry of music. The subject of this work—an inlet along the English Channel—is obscured by the approaching night, allowing Whistler to fully explore the tonal harmonies of darkness.

entries.title: The Millinery Shop
entries.creator: Hilaire Germain Edgar Degas
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: When this work was painted, millinery work (hat making) was considered a prestigious trade, elevating the women who succeeded in the business. Degas addressed this subtle shift in the class hierarchy: He gave his milliner a dress nice enough to be worn by an affluent woman, and though she does not wear the expected hat of a high-class lady, Degas playfully positioned the hat with green trimmings so it seems to sit atop the woman’s head.

entries.title: Old Man with a Gold Chain
entries.creator: Rembrandt van Rijn
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: In his character studies, Rembrandt explored the effect of a single figure, made dramatic through the use of rich, subtle lighting and costumes, which the artist collected to transform his models. Here, the gold chain and steel gorget suggest an honored military career, while the plumed beret evokes an earlier time. The unidentified sitter, once thought to be the artist’s father, was a favorite model.

entries.title: Mountain Brook
entries.creator: Albert Bierstadt
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: Albert Bierstadt is best remembered for his paintings of the American West, but during his early career, the ambitious artist also created New England landscapes, particularly of the White Mountains, as seen here. When this painting was first exhibited in 1863, critics declared it Bierstadt’s “best work” and praised the artist’s skillful contrast of “light and shade,” which brings a heightened realism to the image.

entries.title: Arlésiennes (Mistral)
entries.creator: Paul Gauguin
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: One of 17 canvases that Paul Gauguin completed during a brief and tumultuous visit with Vincent van Gogh in Arles, this powerful and enigmatic painting depicts the public garden directly across from Van Gogh’s house. The painting's large, ﬂat areas of color, arbitrary handling of space, and enigmatic silhouettes exemplify the deliberateness with which Gauguin sought visual harmony and symbolism in his work.

entries.title: Magnolias on Light Blue Velvet Cloth
entries.creator: Martin Johnson Heade
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: This painting dates from the later part of Martin Johnson Heade’s long, varied, and peripatetic career. After traveling through the United States, to England and continental Europe, and three different times to Brazil, Heade settled in Saint Augustine, Florida, at the age of 64. There he began painting detailed arrangements of native flowers, including the Cherokee rose, orange blossom, and, as in this work, magnolia.

entries.title: The Assumption of the Virgin
entries.creator: Domenico Theotokópoulos, called El Greco
entries.rights: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
entries.description: This painting was the central element of an altarpiece that was El Greco’s ﬁrst major Spanish commission and large public work. The Virgin ﬂoats upward on the crescent moon, a symbol of her purity, while the apostles express amazement and concern. El Greco’s broad brushstrokes and bold color made this painting a favorite of modern artists such as Pablo Picasso and Mary Cassatt.
